pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. content.text:
**Short answer:** about an afternoon to get the Pi pairing and reading live data, and one more evening to make it reconnect by itself every time the car starts. Both depend on which adapter you bought, because one type of Bluetooth adapter makes this much harder (below).

## Time estimate (you and Lance together)

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Pair once from the Pi (`bluetoothctl`: scan, pair, trust), then send `ATZ` and `010C` by hand and see an RPM reply | 1–3 hours |
| Auto-reconnect: the daemon opens the connection itself and retries in a loop until the adapter answers | 3–6 hours, mostly key-on/key-off testing in the CR-V |
| **Total** | **Half a day to a full day** |
| If the adapter turns out to be BLE-only (see below) | Add 1–2 days, or return it |

This covers only the connection. The Mode 01 reader in C has to be written either way; Bluetooth doesn't change that work much.

## Can it pair once and then connect by itself?

Yes. Pairing and marking the adapter as trusted is a one-time step, and the pairing survives reboots. After that, the reader daemon opens a Bluetooth serial socket straight to the adapter's address, from our own C code with no helper tools. When the connection drops, it retries every few seconds. At key-on the Pi boots, the daemon starts, and within a few seconds it is reading. Losing the connection at key-off is just another error our code handles, which fits the "survives restarts" rule we already have.

## Things to check first

1. **Is the adapter Bluetooth Classic or BLE-only?** Cheap adapters sold as "iPhone compatible" are often BLE-only. They don't show up as a serial device, so our C code would have to speak the BLE protocol (GATT) directly, and that is where the extra days go. Classic adapters (most "Android" ELM327s, OBDLink LX) are the easy case. Send me the model name or listing and I'll tell you which one it is.

# Mini design overview: OBD2 over Bluetooth (OBDLink LX)

**The build:** the adapter stays plugged into the CR-V's OBD2 port and sleeps while the car is off. At key-on, the 12 V socket powers the Pi, the Pi boots, and our C daemon connects to the adapter over Bluetooth. It sends Mode 01 requests about 10 times a second and writes every sample to the SD card in a way that survives the power cut. At key-off the power dies, and the next boot recovers the log. The owner's phone joins the Pi's own Wi-Fi to see the status page.

```
[CR-V OBD2 port] ─(BT Classic, serial)─▶ [Pi: reader → store → analysis] ─(Wi-Fi hotspot)─▶ phone
[12 V socket] ── USB-C 5V/3A+ ──────────▶ [Pi]   (power cut at key-off = mechanism D's test)
```

## Cost

| Item | USD |
|---|---|
| OBDLink LX | 50–70 |
| 12 V → USB-C charger (3 A+) and cable | 15–25 |
| High-endurance microSD | 10–15 |
| **Subtotal if you already own a Pi** | **~75–110** |
| Raspberry Pi 4/5, if needed | +55–80 |
| USB Bluetooth dongle, only if needed | +10–15 |

With the OBDLink SX (USB) instead, the total is about $20–30 less.

## Timeline

Today is 9/23. **M2 is due 10/11, and baseline collection has to start by then.**

| When | What | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| This week | Buy the parts and flash the Pi. Check that the 12 V socket turns off with the key. | 1–2 h |
| First evening with parts | Pair the adapter, send commands by hand, and **run the PID survey** (D-006) | 2–3 h |
| Next 3–5 days | C reader with auto-reconnect, and a first version of the logger that survives power cuts | 8–12 h |
| By 10/11 | Leave it logging on Lance's daily drives | Almost no effort, but calendar time |
| After that | The analysis runs on real data that keeps piling up | Covered by the M3/M4 plan |

## Difficulty

| Part | Difficulty | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Pairing and sending commands by hand | Easy | Standard tools, and the LX is well behaved |
| Bluetooth socket and reconnect loop in C | Easy–medium | Short code. The edge cases are the hard part. |
| Mode 01 request/reply parsing | Medium | Timeouts, `NO DATA`, replies spread over several lines |
| Surviving power cuts (D) | **Hard** | This is the graded part, whatever the adapter is |
| Supervisor (E) | Medium–hard | Exit codes, heartbeats, surviving `kill -9` |

## Where the time goes

1. **Testing in the car.** Each test is a key cycle in Lance's CR-V. Bugs that only happen in the car cost a scheduling round-trip, not minutes. Fix: record the raw adapter output early, then replay it on a laptop (`make replay`).
2. **PID survey results.** If the CR-V doesn't report oil temperature through standard Mode 01, the fault list and detection plan change. That could mean days of rework, so **run the survey first.**
3. **Boot time at key-on.** The Pi takes about 20–40 s to boot and connect, and the first part of engine warm-up is lost in that window. Warm-up is one of the signals we diagnose from. Measure it early, and decide whether to shorten boot or just record the gap.
4. **Reconnect edge cases.** The adapter waking slower than the Pi, a half-open connection after key-off, BlueZ caching old state. Each one is small, but each needs a key cycle to reproduce.
5. **Wi-Fi hotspot and Bluetooth on one radio.** Probably fine. If it isn't, it shows up as random dropouts that are slow to trace. The $12 dongle is the escape hatch.
6. **Time waiting on driving.** Baselines need weeks of normal driving. That's why starting logging before 10/11 matters more than polishing the code.
7. **Paperwork.** Going Bluetooth means a new decision entry replacing D-015, plus updates to the BOM, wiring and setup docs. Budget about an hour. With the SX, none of this is needed.

**My take:** the LX is the easiest hardware choice, but the adapter isn't where the risk is. The PID survey and the time it takes to collect driving data decide whether we're on schedule, so get the parts and run the survey this week.

# D. Intelligence and analysis

## D.1 — Self-trained model; training in Python, inference in C 🔒
`D-004` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden (confirmed with instructor) · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

A locally-trained, self-authored model is permitted; hosted APIs and third-party
pretrained weights are not. Therefore: training in `tools/train/`, weights versioned under
`models/` with the training commit in the header, **inference in C in `src/analysis/`**, no
network at runtime.

**Why inference in C.** First and most important for the grade: the runtime path sits
inside the supervised multi-process architecture, and a Python process there muddies the
boundary a grader must verify in sixty seconds. Second: it removes an interpreter, a
garbage collector and ~30 MB of RSS from a 48-hour memory-stability test we are graded on.

**What the model is not doing.** The features are the intelligence — operating-point
binning, per-bin baselines, Mahalanobis residuals, Theil–Sen trends, all hand-written.
Delete the weights file and the system still produces residuals and trends; it loses only
the final labeling step. That separation is deliberate and it is the answer at the defense.

## D.2 — Analysis pipeline shape 🔒
Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

Operating-point binning (RPM × load × coolant temp) → per-bin running mean/variance →
multivariate residual (Mahalanobis) → robust trend (Theil–Sen) → classifier → state
machine with hysteresis and dwell.

**Why binning comes first.** Comparing a cold idle to a warm cruise is a false-alarm
generator. Every comparison happens inside one bin, against genuinely comparable
conditions. This single step removes more false positives than anything else downstream.

**Why multivariate.** The signal is the *correlation between sensors*, not any single
sensor's value — oil pressure is supposed to rise with RPM. A measure of anomaly that
already accounts for normal partnerships, and alarms only when a partnership breaks, is
what makes this something a threshold provably cannot do (handout §3.3).

## D.3 — Hysteresis and dwell before any verdict surfaces 🔒
Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

No verdict reaches the user until it has persisted. Trip and un-trip levels differ
deliberately.

**Why.** A monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged, and an unplugged monitor is worse
than none because someone far away believes it is on duty. **False-positive rate is a
first-class metric in `docs/EVALUATION.md`, not an afterthought.**

## D.4 — The threshold test, as a standing rule 🔒
Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

Every diagnostic we ship must require at least two cooperating sensors to reach its
conclusion. If a single threshold on a single value could produce the verdict, it is not
intelligence and it does not count. **Write the reason down in `docs/DESIGN.md` when adding a
diagnostic** — this is checked at the defense.

## Part 1: Faking the adapter for test data

**It's easy, as long as you fake it at the right layer.** There are two places you can fake it, and they test different things.

| Layer | How | Effort | What it tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Serial stream (recommended)** | A Python script in `tools/` opens a pty (a fake terminal device) and answers like an ELM327: `ATZ` → `ELM327 v1.4b`, `010C` → `41 0C 1A F8`. The daemon opens the pty instead of the Bluetooth socket. | **2–4 hours** | Everything after the connection: parsing, timeouts, `NO DATA`, storage, analysis, supervisor. Runs on a laptop, in CI, and in the soak. |
| Bluetooth radio | A second Pi or a laptop registers a Bluetooth serial service and runs the same fake-adapter script behind it | **Half a day to a day**, mostly BlueZ service-registration friction | Only pairing, reconnect, and dropout handling |

To the C daemon, a Bluetooth serial socket and a pty are both just a file descriptor to read and write, so the serial-stream fake covers almost all of the code. Use the radio-level fake only to rehearse reconnects, and "adapter vanished" is easier to test by pulling the fake's plug anyway. A ready-made emulator, `ELM327-emulator` on PyPI, might save the first hour. Check its license first. It's allowed in `tools/`, never in `src/`.

This fits the scaffolding already in the repo. `tools/replay.py` already has `--label replay|synth` and a `--speed` option that "compresses a month into an afternoon". The fake adapter is the other half of that: replay feeds recorded drives into the pipeline, and the fake adapter drives the reader itself.

**Three rules that keep it from backfiring:**
1. **Label it.** The daemon can't tell a fake adapter from a real one, so the label can't come from the data. It has to come from how the daemon is started (a config or flag giving the source as `synth`), and it goes on every record (CLAUDE.md §2.7). If one unlabeled synthetic record reaches a baseline, that is an integrity failure, not a bug.
2. **Script the faults the adapter produces, not just clean data.** The value is in reproducing on demand what the CR-V would otherwise make you drive to see: `NO DATA`, `STOPPED`, `CAN ERROR`, replies cut off mid-line, a 3-second silence, the connection dropping in the middle of a request.
3. **Endless fake data checks the plumbing, never the model.** If we generate faults with our own formula and the model finds them, it has learned our formula. Detection rates can only be measured on real recorded drives with faults we actually induced (E.2). Synthetic data is for the soak, stress tests, and regression checks.

## Part 2: What can an ML model really do with this data?

**Honestly: less than "ML" suggests, and that's the design.** At about 1 sample per second per PID, from a few weeks of one car, you get these:

**What works well**
- **Learning normal for each operating condition.** Fuel trim at warm idle, coolant temperature at highway load, warm-up time from a cold start. Most of the value is here, and it's statistics (binning, per-bin baselines, Mahalanobis distance), not a trained model. D-004 already says this.
- **Catching when sensors stop agreeing.** A vacuum leak is the textbook case: long-term fuel trim goes positive at idle and returns to normal under load. Neither value alone crosses a threshold, but the relationship breaks. That passes the D-004 rule that a verdict needs two sensors.
- **Slow trends.** Theil–Sen over weeks catches drift a single drive can't show.
- **Naming the fault (the classifier's actual job).** Given a deviation, it says whether it looks like a mixture problem, a cooling problem, or a sensor fault. With only a handful of labeled induced-fault drives, that should be a **small model**: logistic regression or a shallow decision tree over our computed features. Anything bigger just memorizes the few drives.

**What it can't do**
- **Anything faster than about 1 Hz.** Misfires, the O2 sensor switching back and forth, knock. The adapter polls too slowly to see them.
- **Remaining life.** "Your thermostat will fail in 3 weeks" needs failures to learn from, and we won't have any. Our claim stays "detects the three faults we induce, with these measured error rates."
- **Anything no sensor measures.** Brake pads, oil condition, belts.
- **Reliable detection in the first weeks.** Until every operating-condition bin has enough data, verdicts should say "still learning", not guess.

## ⚠️ Something that came up while checking this
Diagnostic #1 in E.1 is **oil pressure degradation**. Standard Mode 01 has **no oil pressure PID**, and our own notes (DECISIONS.md A.2) already say the CR-V may only have an oil pressure *switch*. If the PID survey confirms that, diagnostic #1 can't be built on this hardware, and one of the three faults has to be replaced (open issue `oilq`). That's one more reason to run the survey the day the adapter arrives. It decides which ML features we build at all.

If you want, the fake adapter can be the first board item after the parts order. It unblocks testing the C reader before anyone gets in the car.

## Is the problem solved with a different framing?

**The framing is right, but "the market is there" and "the problem is solved" are both further than we can back up yet.** Three corrections:

1. **Market.** We haven't checked it. Consumer OBD2 apps mostly read trouble codes after the check-engine light is on. Fleet telematics companies already sell predictive maintenance. "Learns one car's normal and flags slow drift for an ordinary owner" may be an open niche, but we have no evidence either way. `docs/PROBLEM.md` should state it as a hypothesis, not a finding.
2. **Most of this framing is already the design.** D-004 already says the baseline features are the real intelligence and the classifier only attaches the label. Leaning on "learn normal, catch slow drift" isn't a pivot, it's saying what we already built more honestly. The part that *would* change is E.1's claim wording. That decision is 🔒 LOCKED, so rewording it needs an explicit yes from both of you, and Lance hasn't reviewed it.
3. **The gap to be upfront about: we can't measure *slow* degradation in one semester.** Nothing on the CR-V will wear out on command by December. What we can measure:
   - **False alarm rate** on weeks of normal driving: real, and the most important number.
   - **Detection of faults we induce ourselves** (vacuum leak, cardboard over the radiator, an unplugged sensor): real, but these faults appear suddenly, not slowly.
   - **Detection of slow drift**: only by replaying real drives with a gradual drift injected into them. That data is labeled `synth`, and EVALUATION.md has to say so plainly.

   "Catches slow drift" will be backed by synthetic evidence. That's defensible if we say it that way, and embarrassing at the defense if we don't.

The "rough guide to the issue" is fine, as long as it's still measurable. The output should be a fault family plus how confident the model is ("mixture, likely an intake leak, moderate confidence"). Then we can compute how often the family is right on the induced faults.

## How hard is training for you two?

**The model is the easy part. Collecting the labeled data is the hard part.**

| Piece | What it is | Difficulty | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| Learning normal (the baselines) | Not really training: a running mean and covariance per operating condition, updated live in C | **Medium.** The math is short. The hard parts are choosing the operating-condition bins, bins with too little data, and the covariance matrix breaking down with few samples (fix: blend it toward the diagonal, "shrinkage") | 8–12 h |
| Slow trends | Theil–Sen slope over a sliding window | Easy–medium | 3–5 h |
| Classifier training | Logistic regression or a shallow decision tree on ~10–15 of our computed features, in Python in `tools/train/` | **Easy.** Intro-course level | 3–5 h |
| Classifier in C | Logistic regression is a dot product plus a sigmoid, ~30 lines. A tree becomes generated `if` statements. | Easy | 2–4 h |
| **Labeled data** | Lance induces each fault on purpose, about **10–20 episodes per fault type**, and we record exactly when each fault starts and stops | **Hard.** No code, but the most time, and it's all on Lance's car and Lance's calendar | 6–10 h of deliberate sessions, spread over weeks |
| Evaluation | False alarm rate per hour, detection rate, time to detect | Medium. This is where points are won or lost | 4–6 h |

**About 25–40 hours of code between you, plus a few weeks of calendar time for data.** That fits inside the M3/M4 hours in `milestones.md`.

**Where students usually lose points:**
- **Splitting train/test by sample instead of by drive.** Samples one second apart are nearly identical, so a random split tests the model on data it has already seen and reports 99% accuracy. **Always split by whole drive.** This is the single most common mistake.
- **Too big a model.** With about 50 labeled episodes, a neural network memorizes them. Keep it small enough that you can defend every weight.
- **Unlabeled synthetic data getting into training.** Every record carries `src=`, so the training script should refuse `synth` unless told otherwise, and then report it.
- **Waiting too long to induce faults.** Each episode needs a scheduled session in Lance's car. Start them in October, not November.
